item.title: Why is Labour Friends of Israel not led by Labour members?
item.dc:creator: DECLASSIFIED STAFF
item.description:
The pro-Israel group does not have to declare its funders because majority of board are not Labour party members

The post Why is Labour Friends of Israel not led by Labour members? appeared first on Declassified UK.
item.content:encoded:
The majority of people on the Labour Friends of Israel (LFI) board are not Labour party members, it has emerged.

This means the group does not have to tell the Electoral Commission who has donated to the organisation, journalist Solomon Hughes revealed today in the Morning Star. 

LFI has sent dozens of Labour MPs on trips to Israel, and UK government ministers regularly speak at its events.

Under UK law, organisations that seek to influence Labour policy and are run mostly by party members are classed as “member’s associations”.

They must register all incoming donations above the current threshold of around £12,000 with the commission.

Campaigner Andrew Feinstein has previously told Declassified that LFI was “very influential in the Labour Party and British politics…Given this influence it is very problematic that their donors remain secret”.

‘Toxic environment’

The Electoral Commission approached LFI in 2024 and 2025 to check if it was a member’s association, according to documents Hughes obtained under freedom of information.

The commission said the group told it that “While some of LFI’s board of directors are members of the Labour party, they do not form a majority on the board. LFI indicated that they monitored directors’ party membership regularly to confirm this.”

This means it does not have to identify its donors. It denies receiving Israeli government funds. 

Four out of five of LFI’s board members have public ties to the Labour Party, including ex-MP Louise Ellman. 

LFI told Hughes that while the majority of its board are not members of the Labour Party, none of them are “a member, or supporter of, any other political party.”

However, until his death last year, the LFI board included a sixth director – millionaire property developer Sir David Garrard – who donated to two of Labour’s political rivals (the Liberal Democrats and The Independent Group) in 2019 while on LFI’s board.

LFI indicated that reasons for their non-Labour Party leadership included “many British Jews felt unable to become members of the Labour party due to the toxic antisemitic environment which existed under Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership”.

Garrard quit the Labour party in early 2018 over Corbyn’s leadership, saying he no longer felt “any affinity or connection” with the party, and became a director of LFI at the end of that year.

Once Keir Starmer became Labour’s leader in 2020, Garrard said he would rejoin the party and is known to have sponsored several LFI events over the next few years.

RELATED

Trade Secretary accused of ‘egregious’ rules breach over Israel links

 READ MORE 

‘Unconvincing’

In his Morning Star column, Hughes commented: “While antisemitism is a real and significant problem in the UK, including the Labour Party, I do not myself believe Labour had a ‘toxic antisemitic environment’ under Corbyn. 

“However, even for those who do believe in this ‘toxic environment’, I find this argument unconvincing because Corbyn stopped being leader in 2020. Many of the five-member LFI Board have clearly been active in, or positive about, the party post-Corbyn. 

“As well as Louise Ellman, who publicly rejoined Labour in 2021, the LFI board includes a Labour activist who was elected as a Camden Councillor in 2022. 

“They are joined by a lobbyist who is currently described by her company as a ‘former Special Adviser to the Prime Minister Andy Burnham’ and a corporate marketing boss who helped found the ‘Labour Women in Business Network’. 

“I find it hard to accept these four people all find themselves unable to join the Labour Party while running Labour Friends of Israel.”

Two-state solution

According to an Electoral Commission document, LFI reported £175,000 worth of donations between 2002 and 2025, however the source of funds was not stated.

The money was used to send Labour politicians on visits to Israel and the West Bank, which have included meeting Israel’s president Isaac Herzog who a UN commission accuses of inciting genocide in Gaza.

LFI says it supports a two-state solution and has promoted Israel’s Democrat party leader Yair Golan ahead of this month’s election against Benjamin Netanyahu.

Despite its opposition to Netanyahu, LFI was critical of steps Labour took to censure Israel’s attacks on Gaza. It opposed the partial arms embargo and recognition of Palestine, and questioned sanctions on trade with illegal settlements.

Hughes said LFI are also “currently campaigning for Labour to ‘bolster’ the ‘defence and security relationship between Israel and the UK’ with military cooperation and ensuring ‘Israel remains a major supplier of arms to the UK’.”

The post Why is Labour Friends of Israel not led by Labour members? appeared first on Declassified UK.

item.title: Trump kidnapped Venezuela’s president. Now Britain looks to profit
item.dc:creator: Ana Maria Monjardino
item.description:
BP and Shell are cashing in on Venezuela’s oil and gas following the kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro.

The post Trump kidnapped Venezuela’s president. Now Britain looks to profit appeared first on Declassified UK.
item.content:encoded:
Britain’s energy giants stand to make huge profits in Venezuela amid a major diplomatic rapprochement between London and Caracas, it can be revealed.

It comes in the wake of the kidnapping of Nicolás Maduro earlier this year in a move described by UN experts as a “deliberate violation of the most fundamental principles of international law”.

Donald Trump has repeatedly emphasised how the US intervention was motivated by oil interests, even telling the UN General Assembly last week: “To the victor belong the spoils”.

Hours after Maduro’s seizure, Keir Starmer said Britain was “not involved”, but refused to be drawn on whether it was unlawful. “We shed no tears about the end of the regime,” he declared.

The kidnapping is already resulting in a boon for Britain’s energy giants, with interim president Delcy Rodríguez welcoming foreign companies back to Venezuela and softening the country’s hydrocarbon legislation.

Since January 2026, BP and Shell have signed major agreements with the Venezuelan government as it appears to be operating under duress from the Trump administration.

Documents obtained by Declassified indicate how Britain’s Foreign Office has helped facilitate their return, with an influx of high-level meetings between executives and officials taking place in the weeks and months after Maduro’s removal.

The opening of Venezuela’s economy has also paved the way for the normalisation of relations between London and Caracas. Plans were made earlier this month to upgrade diplomatic representation to ambassadorial level.

But serious questions surround benefitting from the kidnapping of a head of state amid a broader assault on Venezuela’s sovereignty.

“US coercive control over Venezuela’s oil revenues may have involved violations of Venezuela’s sovereignty”, said UN special rapporteur Ben Saul.

That includes breaches of “the duty of non-intervention, the right of economic self-determination, and the principle of permanent sovereignty over natural resources”.

Professor Francisco Rodríguez, a leading Venezuelan economist who has advised its national assembly, told Declassified that “deals of this type are much more likely to survive when there is a broad consensus not only on their legal validity but on their desirability for the nation.

“At present, I see many more sectors of Venezuelan society that do not consider these agreements either legal or convenient for the nation, and some of them see them as outright exploitative”.

Rodríguez added: “It is hard to see any truly autonomous Venezuelan leaders signing these deals were a gun not pointed at their head”.

RELATED

One hundred years of British interference in Venezuela

 READ MORE 

Firesale

Venezuela’s economy has been restructured under Delcy Rodríguez, who assumed power in January and was pictured with Trump earlier this month in New York, just miles from Maduro’s prison cell.

The country’s hydrocarbon legislation has been modified to make the terms more favourable for foreign firms, and its energy revenues are now being diverted through the US Treasury, with Washington taking a major cut.

By July, the US government had collected more than $13 billion in revenues from Venezuelan oil sales, according to the Financial Times.

In August, Trump also announced a “historic oil agreement” with Venezuela which would give the US control of more than 65 billion barrels of oil reserves for 100 years.

The deal would secure “our energy dominance for the next century”, Trump declared, “all at zero cost to the United States”. 

Remarkably, the company at the forefront of that agreement, North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP), hired three lawyers who had previously worked for the UK’s Serious Fraud Office.

It is within this context that Shell and BP have returned to Venezuela.

Shell has been granted concessions to develop and operate two offshore gas fields, named Loran and Dragon, which are projected to contain vast amounts of recoverable gas.

The company also signed a preliminary deal to develop two onshore oil fields known as Carito and Pirital in Monagas State, one of the country’s most oil-rich regions. 

After signing a memorandum of understanding (MoU) in Caracas in March, Shell’s regional manager Adam Lowmass recalled the company’s “long history in Venezuela, dating from 1912”. He declared: “I could not be prouder of our team”.

BP signed its own MoU with the Venezuelan government in April to develop the Cocuina-Manakin gas field which sits on the maritime border with Trinidad and Tobago.

The company was also granted a licence for the second phase of operations on the Loran field in partnership with Emirati XRG and Qatari UCC Oil and Gas, and has started trading oil in the US.

Shell and BP plan to process Venezuela’s natural gas using the Atlantic LNG plant and export terminal in Trinidad and Tobago, in which they are both major shareholders.

This cross-border presence will give the firms significant control over the supply chain of natural gas in the Caribbean, a large portion of which will be destined for Europe.

Meetings and lobbying

Data obtained by Declassified through the Freedom of Information Act indicates how the Foreign Office has facilitated Shell and BP’s return to Venezuela.

Executives from the companies met with Colin Dick, Britain’s chargé d’affaires in Caracas, eight times in the two months following Maduro’s kidnapping, compared with eight meetings for all of 2025.

While the Foreign Office has refused to disclose what was discussed beyond a few heavily redacted emails, the frequency of the meetings might be seen as implicit endorsement for the energy giants’ new ventures in Venezuela.

Oil has been guiding British foreign policy in Venezuela for over a century. Former foreign minister for the Americas Alan Duncan declared in 2018: “The revival of the oil industry will be an essential element in any recovery, and I can imagine that British companies like Shell and BP will want to be part of it”.

Britain’s current director for the Americas Harriet Thompson was in Caracas in early March 2026 as Shell was gearing up to sign major new energy deals.

Thompson “conducted a productive visit that included meetings at the Venezuelan Foreign Ministry and engagements with representatives of British companies to explore growth opportunities for both countries”, the embassy said.

When asked in parliament whether those talks involved British natural resource companies, the Foreign Office said the question had already been answered in January – two months before the meetings had even taken place.

In its own write-up, the Venezuelan government said the delegation was the first of its kind for years, and opened new routes for “trade exchange” within a broader goal of “strengthening cooperation in strategic sectors”.

Earlier this month, Venezuela’s foreign minister and former ambassador to the UK Félix Plasencia and National Assembly president Jorge Rodríguez, Delcy’s brother, were in London for another high-level diplomatic exchange.

Standing outside the Foreign Office, Rodríguez noted how the meetings with British diplomats had covered “oil and gas investments” and the “rapid economic growth of Venezuela”. 

RELATED

Secretive UK team met in Venezuela to promote British energy...

 READ MORE 

‘Plundering’

BP and Shell have also been busy lobbying on Venezuela in Washington after a long period of relative dormancy. 

Their efforts have focussed on convincing the US Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to give them licences to operate in Venezuela as the Trump administration eases sanctions for projects which benefit US oil interests.

In the first quarter of 2026, Shell registered lobbying activities worth $1.3 million in the US which involved “the commercial development of natural gas in the Dragon gas field offshore Venezuela and Trinidad and Tobago pursuant to a licence issued by OFAC”.

During the same period, BP registered $1.18 million in US lobbying activities which included a focus on “Venezuela and OFAC licensing”.

Shell’s CEO Wael Sawan even met with Trump in January, saying he was “ready to go” with “a few billion dollars’ worth of opportunities to invest” in Venezuela.

Days later, US lawmakers implored Sawan and other oil executives “to decline to participate in any transaction or arrangement that relies on the Trump Administration’s asserted authority to control Venezuelan oil assets”.

Ricardo Vaz, lead editor of Venezuela Analysis, told Declassified: “Much like it joined the US in its economic blockade, the UK and UK-headquartered corporations are determined not to miss out on the plundering of Venezuela’s natural resources in this post-January 3 context.

“BP and Shell have been on the frontlines to take advantage of the reformed energy sector and feature among the six corporations that received the first general licence to negotiate deals with the Venezuelan government.

“Both companies had an extensive operational history in Venezuela’s oil industry, and they will now arguably return in the most favourable conditions they have ever enjoyed”.

Diplomatic rapprochement

The improved position of BP and Shell in Venezuela has coincided with a significant diplomatic rapprochement between London and Caracas.

Under Maduro, the UK government insisted fresh elections were necessary before diplomatic normalisation, but the position has now been reversed, with the Foreign Office saying a democratic transition requires improved diplomatic relations.

“Upgrading our relations will strengthen our ability to play a constructive role in support of a democratic transition” and “promote UK businesses in Venezuela”, foreign minister Chris Elmore said earlier this month.

This “upgrade”, he said, would pave the way for the appointment of a UK ambassador in Caracas for the first time since 2017.

To celebrate this new spring in the UK-Venezuela partnership, Delcy Rodríguez met with Britain’s chargé d’affaires Colin Dick in Caracas on 18 September. The pair were filmed laughing together as they fed deer and admired peacocks.

“Venezuela and the United Kingdom are opening a new chapter in their bilateral relations”, beamed Rodríguez.

RELATED

Alternatives: How to end our addiction to oil and gas

 READ MORE 

The frozen gold 

One of Venezuela’s top priorities amid the improvement of diplomatic relations will be the return of roughly $4 billion of gold that has been frozen in the Bank of England for over seven years.

While Elmore said Britain’s “long-standing position is to recognise states, not governments”, it was the UK government’s decision to recognise a parallel government under Venezuelan opposition figure Juan Guaidó in 2019 that fomented the gold deadlock.

According to former US National Security Adviser John Bolton, then foreign secretary Jeremy Hunt was “delighted” to help with Washington’s destabilisation campaign in Venezuela, “for example freezing Venezuelan gold deposits in the Bank of England”.

After a protracted legal battle over ownership of the assets, Guaidó was ousted and his parallel government dissolved in 2022 – but the gold remained frozen due to Britain’s enduring non-recognition of Maduro.

The Rodríguez administration and the Venezuelan opposition have since engaged in negotiations, with both sides reportedly agreeing that the gold should be released.

These negotiations, according to the Financial Times, might result in the gold being transferred from the Bank of England to the Federal Reserve of New York, with the assets only available as collateral for government borrowing rather than for sale.

Transferring the gold to the country whose leader orchestrated the kidnapping of Venezuela’s head of state – after freezing the gold amid concerns about democratic legitimacy – might raise awkward questions for the Foreign Office and the Bank of England.

A spokesperson for the Bank of England previously said: “The Bank is not in a position to act on instructions until there is a further order from the UK Court which makes clear who has legal authority over the account. This requires the parties involved in the case to approach the UK Court to settle the dispute”.

The Foreign Office, BP, and Shell were approached for comment.

The post Trump kidnapped Venezuela’s president. Now Britain looks to profit appeared first on Declassified UK.

item.title: British soldiers interrogated detainees before mass execution
item.dc:creator: Amaar Chowdhury
item.description:
UK helped Gulf monarchy crackdown on dissidents to keep control over Strait of Hormuz oil route

The post British soldiers interrogated detainees before mass execution appeared first on Declassified UK.
item.content:encoded:
British soldiers interrogated dissidents in Oman before nearly a dozen of the men were executed in 1973, newly discovered files show.

Although Britain had abolished the death penalty for almost all offences four years prior to the executions, UK troops on loan to the Sultan of Oman were embroiled in his own use of capital punishment.

Sultan Qaboos, a Gulf autocrat, relied on British help to capture around 90 people in 1972-73 suspected of being part of the Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arabian Gulf (PFLOAG).

They were a left-wing group which sought democracy, women’s liberation and socialism in the southern Dhufar region of Oman.

The PFLOAG was seen as a threat to British oil interests in Oman, a Gulf state which controls half of the Strait of Hormuz.

The crackdown, codenamed Operation Jason, saw a temporary interrogation centre established in Sur, 100 kilometres away from the capital Muscat.

As part of Operation Jason, the British sent over a Major R Willingale from the Royal Signals to lead a six man “intelligence collation team”. [1]

Although Willingale was formally there to install monitoring equipment in the interrogation rooms at Sur, the team was still allowed to conduct “secondary questioning” of which would apparently “not include any form of ill-treatment.”

Britain had previously tortured other detainees in Oman in 1971. This time, the British personnel could only put “gentlemanly” questioning to over 77 rebels accused of plotting an insurrection. 

There appear to be no detailed records from the interrogation in the UK National Archives. 

However, PFLOAG officials claimed in their weekly pamphlets that “brutal torture operations” led to a number of individuals facing “amputations in addition to the development of various diseases”, and that a pregnant woman held in detention had died as a result of the “torture practised by the British and Jordanian intelligence services.”

RELATED

When Britain used torture to control the Strait of Hormuz

 READ MORE 

Executed

Sultan Qaboos went on to approve the death penalty for several of the rebels interrogated by British officers on loan to his army.

Declassified has cross-referenced records in the National Archives with those published by legal scholars in Oman to identify the names of 11 of those executed. The full list is below. [2]

One of the men, Hamad Majid Al-Mukhaini, had previously been a lieutenant in the Sultan’s Armed Forces, but “off-hand treatment by British officers” caused him to defect to the PFLOAG, according to the British ambassador to Oman, Donald Hawley.

It took only one day of court proceedings for the judge, Sayyid Sultan Bin Hamoud Al-Busaidi, to sentence those 11 people to death in June 1973.

Ambassador Hawley’s meagre attempts to appeal to Qaboos for clemency of those convicted were entirely unsuccessful.

It appears that the goal was in-fact to cover their own backs. “We should not wish any British personnel, whether contract, seconded or BATT [British Army Training Team] to be involved in executions,” Douglas-Home wrote to Hawley.

They were all executed a week later, despite the PFLOAG’s threat being greatly exaggerated. 

“All the indications are that [the PFLOAG] was in no shape to organise the overthrow of the present regime,” according to British diplomat Sir Terence Clarke writing back to the Foreign Office.

Sultan Qaboos met Britain’s then prime minister, Conservative Edward Heath, in Downing Street three months after the executions.

The PFLOAG eventually lost the Dhufar war, leaving Sultan Qaboos to rule Oman for half a century. 

The UK ambassador to Muscat would explain in 1980 that control of the “oil-important Straits of Hormuz, is what the Dhufar War was all about.” 

NOTES:

[1] UK intelligence team was composed of: JE Gooch (chief technician, RAF), Sergeant RJ Yarnell, Sergeant R Bumstead, Sergeant JA Ryles and Sergeant DA Langham.

[2] The men executed were: Hamad Majid Al-Mukhaini, Khalfan Salem Al-Wahibi, Ali Thani Khalaf Al-Jamoudi, Hamoud Ahmed Al-Rahbi, Mohammed Saeed Saeed Al-Wahibi, Hamoud Hamid Al-Ghasani, Mohammed Talib Sulaiman Al-Busaidi, Mohammed Hashim Al-Tai, Ali Mohammed Salem Al-Marzouqi, Mubarak Hamad Al-Kitani, and Said Abdullah Hamad Al-Alawi.

Note: Arabic names might differ in spelling following translation into English

The post British soldiers interrogated detainees before mass execution appeared first on Declassified UK.

item.title: I was a senior British army lawyer. This is the truth about ‘lawfare’
item.dc:creator: Nicholas Mercer
item.description:
Concerns about elderly Northern Ireland veterans are being used to protect the SAS from the Afghanistan inquiry

The post I was a senior British army lawyer. This is the truth about ‘lawfare’ appeared first on Declassified UK.
item.content:encoded:
The last Conservative government passed the Legacy Act, which shut down many routes to justice for victims of the Troubles in Northern Ireland.

Inquests were stopped, even when British soldiers fired the fatal shots.

Labour’s manifesto pledged to pass a Troubles Bill which would reverse some of the worst excesses of the Legacy Act.

Already, this has sparked a backlash. Conservative MP and former SAS soldier David Davis wants action to protect troops who “no longer fear only the enemy in front of them but the lawyer behind them.” 

However, there are other voices in this debate which have not been heard, including members of the armed forces who have served in Northern Ireland and take a different view.

I am one of them.

Earlier this month, I spoke at an event in Parliament organised by Amnesty International and the Centre for Military Justice.

Politicians we met expressed surprise at hearing military voices challenge what has too often been presented as a unanimous chorus of calls for impunity provisions to be reintroduced into the Troubles Bill.

The choreographed narrative has been accompanied by a marked failure of analysis. Many of the allegations simply do not stack up. 

Indeed, this might be because the so-called “objections” to the Troubles Bill have very little to do with Northern Ireland and more a desire to escape the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR), not least in the light of recent revelations regarding UK Special Forces in Afghanistan.

RELATED

Hero’s funeral for ex-soldier is an insult to real victim

 READ MORE 

Floodgates

First and foremost, there are a number of popular myths in this debate about the Troubles Bill which seem to have been accepted as “facts”, but which are never challenged.

The first of these is that troops will be subjected to “vexatious” litigation if this bill is passed into law. We have been here before. 

The word found its way into the Conservative Party manifesto 2019 and then into the supposed rationale for the Overseas Operations Bill 2020. 

However, this allegation was explored by the Joint Committee on Human Rights at the time who concluded that they were unaware of any such cases against UK forces and called upon ministers not to use “politicised and inaccurate language”. 

Nevertheless, the term “vexatious” has returned once again.

As well as the myth of “vexatious” litigation, there is also the myth of “opening the floodgates”.

However, as Professor Kieron McEvoy recently said in the Irish Times “between 2012 and 2024, there were 25 decisions to prosecute conflict-related offences in Northern Ireland, six of which were against soldiers. Only one ex-soldier was convicted of manslaughter… actual data often appears to be beside the point”. 

The ECHR has been part of our domestic law since 1997 but has not “opened the flood gates” so why should it now? 

Immune

As to the allegation that the IRA have somehow obtained “immunity from prosecution”, Lady Justice Hallett has already pointed out that the so-called “comfort letters” do not amount to “a get out of jail free card”. 

There were no amnesties.

The Conservative Government’s 2023 Legacy Act sought to create an immunity scheme for those who might be prosecuted for alleged offences committed during the Troubles. It would apply to service personnel (as well as terrorists). 

A similar scheme was devised for the Overseas Operations Bill 2020, that would have effectively placed service personnel accused of war crimes outside the reach of the law in certain circumstances, but there was very strong military push back at the time. 

General Sir Nick Carter stated that UK Armed Forces should “uphold the rule of law in the way that it is presented to everyone else”. Lord Guthrie argued that making exceptions for troops ran the risk that their crimes might go unpunished. 

There was also general agreement that carving out exemptions for UK forces did nothing to incentivise good conduct on the battlefield going forward.

So why the objections to the UK government’s current Troubles Bill? 

RELATED

Impunity for killings in service of the state: the UK...

 READ MORE 

Afghanistan inquiry

Perhaps the answer lies elsewhere.

As a result of exposure by Panorama, the SAS now stand accused of committing war crimes in Afghanistan and effecting a cover up. 

None of those allegations would have come to light without the ECHR, and in particular Article 2, which requires an independent investigation when there are allegations of unlawful killing by the state. 

How convenient it would be for the SAS, and other state actors, if the UK were to leave the ECHR entirely so they no longer had to face calls for independent investigations. 

And what better way to disguise the motive than with populist assertions about elderly veterans in Northern Ireland and then laying the blame at the feet of the ECHR?

The great irony is that our special forces or other state actors would not be worried about legacy issues from Afghanistan or indeed Northern Ireland if human rights norms had been applied rigorously at the time. 

Military operations would have been conducted in accordance with the rule of law and there would have been no cover up, because the ECHR would have prevented it. 

There would have been a proper independent inquiry at the time – the guilty would have been dealt with, the innocent exonerated. 

This is precisely why the application of the Human Rights Act is so important – it will stop “legacy” issues arising now and in the future.

The recent events in the Middle East graphically illustrate how the world can spiral out of control when the rules-based order is egregiously ignored. 

This is a compelling argument in itself for the strict adherence to the rule of law in military operations. 

Now is manifestly the time for the UK government to rigorously uphold the rule of law, including human rights, and not to abandon it like some of our “allies” have chosen to do.

The post I was a senior British army lawyer. This is the truth about ‘lawfare’ appeared first on Declassified UK.

item.title: Declassified journalists banned from Labour conference – again
item.dc:creator: Martin Williams
item.description:
Labour MPs have condemned the ‘Trump-like’ decision, saying party is ‘bang out of order’

The post Declassified journalists banned from Labour conference – again appeared first on Declassified UK.
item.content:encoded:
Declassified journalists have been banned from the Labour Party’s annual conference for the third year in a row.

The event in Liverpool next week is the first under new prime minister Andy Burnham and is traditionally an opportunity for reporters to question politicians.

But three Declassified journalists were denied media passes, with the party claiming that they would only be given to those “with a relevant portfolio”. 

The rejection email said: “We reserve the right to reject an application if we cannot find any evidence the applicant is a working journalist or photographer with a political portfolio or working on behalf of a relevant media outlet.”

The ban comes despite all Declassified staff journalists being accredited with the National Union of Journalists (NUJ), while one is also a member of the Parliamentary Press Gallery.

Emails requesting an appeal of the decision – or a refund of the £420 in entry fees – have so far gone unanswered.

The NUJ’s general secretary Laura Davidson called on Labour to rethink its decision, saying: “Journalists must be able to report on and question political parties – especially those who are in power.

“Political parties must demonstrate their commitment to press freedom, freedom of expression and the public’s right to be informed.”

‘Dark hole’

Several Labour MPs have reacted angrily to the ban, with one calling it “Trump-like”. 

Speaking to Declassified, the former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell said: “This Trump-like banning of a significant media player is a demonstration that, at the heart of the Labour Party bureaucracy, Starmer’s Labour Together crew are still in charge.” 

He added: “Andy Burnham and Labour’s new general secretary will need to launch a radical reorganisation of this bureaucracy before they undermine him as they have past leaders.”

Another prominent MP, who asked not to be named, also alluded to the role of the party’s right-wing, saying: “This feels like the decision of some jumped-up old Labour-Right turd, hoping you’ll go away and be banned in a dark hole somewhere.”

RELATED

Declassified wins battle over access to Parliament

 READ MORE 

‘Is this what change looks like?’

Kim Johnson, the MP for Liverpool Riverside where the conference takes place, said the decision to block Declassified was “bang out of order”.

“Declassified is a serious, independent media outlet,” she said. “To suggest they somehow aren’t ‘real journalists’ because Labour doesn’t consider them ‘relevant’ is frankly insulting.”

“We rightly condemn Reform when they ban local journalists from their councils and Donald Trump when he tries to decide which journalists are allowed access to the White House. So why are we seeing the same sort of behaviour from our own political party?”

She added: “I genuinely thought the new regime would represent a change from the Starmer-era tricks of trying to control the message and manage the media to duck accountability. If this is what change looks like, it is looking an awful lot like more of the same.”

Labour backbencher John Trickett said: “It is more than disappointing that Declassified has been banned from the Labour conference this year under Burnham’s new leadership. 

“Legacy media can be very hostile to Labour and yet – rightly – they are allowed to be present. Labour ought to embrace new media outlets as a way of breaking the power of the mainstream media: Andy Burnham ought to reverse the ban.”

Labour peer Prem Sikka also called on his party to review the ban. He told Declassified: “It is very disappointing that Labour is continuing with the practices established under Keir Starmer and barring independent journalists from its conference, a practice associated with Donald Trump.”

“The government must be scrutinised and the ban will not help Andy Burnham to present himself as a candidate for change.”

Clive Lewis, the MP for Norwich South, said: “Declassified UK should be admitted to conference, or Labour should publicly explain, with a credible reason, why it has been excluded. Democracy means accepting scrutiny, especially when it is uncomfortable.”

He added: “Labour needs a clean break with the closed and controlling political culture of the past seven years, and a new culture rooted in democracy, openness and respect for a free press.”

Richard Burgon, Labour MP for Leeds East, said: “Labour should overturn this decision and allow Declassified’s accredited journalists to cover Labour Conference.

“It is the job of journalists to ask awkward questions. At a time when press freedom is increasingly under attack around the world, that role matters more than ever.”

Lobbyists welcome

While barring journalists from the conference, Labour is set to once again welcome a mass of corporate lobbyists – including representatives from major arms companies.

They include Anacta, which has previously lobbied for Pearson Engineering – an arms firm owned by the Israeli government.

The lobbying company will host an entire “hub” inside the conference venue, where senior Labour figures were last year seen drinking with lobbyists and journalists.

Another lobbying firm, Arden Strategies, is hosting an “Insights Hub” and “Events Lounge”, with talks from top government ministers. 

Reporting earlier this year accused Arden Strategies of “selling access to government officials” for tens of thousands of pounds. While not illegal, the arrangement was described as “hugely problematic” by the campaign group Spotlight on Corruption.

Meanwhile, the conference programme suggests that the new defence secretary, Wes Streeting, will do a “one-to-one interview” at an event hosted by the arms giant BAE Systems.

The company has sold military equipment and technology used by the Israeli military.

Labour Friends of Israel will also be returning to the conference with its annual reception, promising “senior cabinet ministers”. 

The group – which is funded by secret donors – organises trips to Israel, where MPs have met the country’s president, Isaac Herzog, and had briefings with the Israeli Defence Forces while the genocide is ongoing.

item.title: UK sanctions on Israel result in no extra arms export suspensions
item.dc:creator: JOHN McEVOY
item.description:
Exclusive: Ed Miliband's ‘double lock’ on arms exports to Israel has made no immediate impact on the flow of weaponry to Tel Aviv.

The post UK sanctions on Israel result in no extra arms export suspensions appeared first on Declassified UK.
item.content:encoded:
The UK government’s new sanctions on Israel have resulted in zero arms export licences being revoked or suspended, it can be revealed.

Earlier this month, Ed Miliband announced a fresh range of measures against Israel including a ban on trade with illegal settlements.

The foreign secretary also addressed arms export licences, declaring that applications for “arms and other exports that materially contribute to the occupation” of Palestine would be refused.

This would amount to a “double lock against arms sales” to Israel, Miliband said.

Over subsequent days, Miliband and other ministers came out to promote the new restrictions, indicating they went much further than Keir Starmer’s ban on 30 out of approximately 350 arms export licences for Israel in 2024.

But information now disclosed to parliament details how the measures have not resulted in any arms export licences for Israel being cancelled or blocked.

In response to a question from Iqbal Mohamed MP, the trade department acknowledged last week how “no additional licences have been revoked or suspended since 8 September 2026”.

This was “largely because licences for items that might materially contribute to the occupation have already been suspended because of Israel’s conduct in the Gaza conflict”.

That the new measures have made no material impact on the flow of military items between London and Tel Aviv has raised concerns that the sanctions have not gone nearly far enough.

Dearbhla Minogue, a lawyer from Global Legal Action Network which took the UK to court over arms exports to Israel, told Declassified: “This appears to mean no concrete consequences for Israel after this government recognised the likelihood of war crimes, ethnic cleansing and what it terms Israeli terrorism”.

Minogue said the government should go further by recognising the risk of genocide in Gaza and do “everything in its power to prevent Israel from completing what it started”.

RELATED

Do Andy Burnham’s sanctions on Israel go far enough?

 READ MORE 

Not far enough

The government insists that many of the extant licences for Israel cover items that are for re-export to a third country or military-grade goods for civilian use such as body armour.

Yet fighter jet components are still being exported to global spares pools used by Israel, and UK-made trainer aircraft parts, which help to sustain the F-35 programme, continue to flow directly to Tel Aviv.

When asked about trainer aircraft, the trade department told parliament that such components “are not used in Gaza and… do not materially contribute to Israel’s illegal occupation”.

This is despite the Foreign Office previously acknowledging that Israel’s M-346 trainer aircraft are “used to train IAF fast-jet pilots” and “facilitate the development of an offensive capacity”.

Martin Butcher, Oxfam’s policy advisor on arms and conflict, said his organisation is concerned that Miliband’s “intent to end UK military support for Israeli authorities’ unlawful occupation of Palestinian territory…is being undermined by a very narrow reading of international law obligations”.

He said the sale of all F-35 and trainer aircraft components to Israel “must stop immediately”.

RELATED

What is the F-35 fighter jet Israel uses to bomb...

 READ MORE 

Enduring military ties 

Despite the sanctions, the Ministry of Defence maintains contracts worth hundreds of millions of pounds with Israeli arms firms which profit from and help sustain the occupation of Palestine.

Just days before Miliband announced the trade sanctions, more than 300 British soldiers were participating in a “landmark” training exercise facilitated by Israel’s largest arms firm, Elbit Systems.

Meanwhile the Israeli state owns the Pearson Engineering arms factory in Newcastle which was recently awarded a £10m contract by the British army.

When asked whether Pearson will be subject to sanctions, the UK government insisted that it wants to “protect legitimate trade between the UK and Israel”.

The decision not to impose a two-way arms embargo also means Israeli weaponry and technology can continue to flow to Britain.

UN trade data recently showed the value of military goods sent from Israel to the UK increased by a factor of more than 100 between 2023 and 2025, from £55,000 to £5.9 million.

Additional concerns about Britain’s arms export licensing regime surround whether UK-made drone engines and other military items are being sent to Israel without any export licence.

Campaign Against Arms Trade media co-ordinator Emily Apple said: “The so-called double lock on arms exports to Israel is nothing more than a soundbite; a smokescreen designed to appease voters, whilst failing to deliver meaningful policy change.

She added: “Business is still booming for UK and Israeli arms companies… Yet again, the government has failed to uphold international law, and failed the Palestinian people”.

The Foreign Office and Department for Trade were approached for comment.

The post UK sanctions on Israel result in no extra arms export suspensions appeared first on Declassified UK.

item.title: What the media isn’t telling you about Burnham’s support for Saudi Arabia
item.dc:creator: IONA CRAIG
item.description:
‘Defensive’ refuelling of planes bombing Yemen can still cause war crimes. Just ask Keir Starmer

The post What the media isn’t telling you about Burnham’s support for Saudi Arabia appeared first on Declassified UK.
item.content:encoded:
Andy Burnham’s decision to send a Royal Air Force plane to Saudi Arabia for “defensive” aerial refuelling in the kingdom’s war against the Houthis has a familiar ring to it. His words echo those of his predecessor.

Keir Starmer provided the same support “to aid self-defence” of the USS Harry S Truman aircraft carrier during Trump’s bombing campaign in Yemen last year.

That “defensive” support began with at least 25 RAF Voyager tanker flights from Akrotiri airbase in Cyprus and ended with RAF fighter jets carrying out a direct strike in April 2025.

RAF Voyagers refuelled US jets during two strikes that the Pentagon said “more likely than not” resulted in 281 civilian casualties, Declassified revealed last week.

Britain’s national press failed to mention our revelation when covering Burnham’s announcement, despite the obvious relevance.

Mission-creep and a lack of transparency over what British support entails similarly surrounds Burnham’s declared support. 

In interviews yesterday to push out the government line, Minister for Defence Procurement Luke Pollard told BBC Radio that the agreement with Saudi Arabia was to “support defensive action” and to “deescalate” the conflict over the Bab al-Mandab waterway. 

He noted that refuelling British-made Typhoon fighter jets used by Saudi Arabia for airstrikes “increases their lethality” and “massively increases their utility”. 

But Pollard would not provide details on what he described as “a range of defensive missions” that have been agreed with Saudi Arabia and acknowledged “a grey” area of what defensive action included.

Reporting by The Times claimed “the remit for Saudi operations goes wider” and includes refuelling of Saudi fighter jets bombing “defensive targets on land and along coastal areas, such as weapons depots and sites used to launch missiles and drones” adding to the opaque nature of Britain’s military support.

‘Think carefully’

British refuelling support to Saudi Arabia, especially if it facilitates Saudi fighter jets carrying out bombing runs into Yemen, risks drawing UK-linked maritime vessels into Houthi targeting criteria. 

Rather than the “de-escalation” of the Arabian Peninsula’s dual shipping lanes that Pollard said motivated the government’s decision, the result may be a significant escalation in particular for British-linked trade. 

Leading Houthi official and politburo member Mohammed al-Bukhaiti told Declassified that the Houthis, also known as Ansarallah, “will not target countries that are not participating in the aggression against Yemen.” 

Commenting further on Thursday morning, al-Bukhaiti said: “We advise Britain to think carefully before becoming involved in the aggression against Yemen. Entering the war will not solve the problem; instead, it will make Britain a party to the conflict and hold it accountable for the consequences.

“Should Britain become involved in the aggression against Yemen in any form, it will bear the consequences, as Yemen will respond in a manner commensurate with the scale and nature of that involvement.”

If the Houthis start to view Britain as a participant in Saudi Arabia’s war and, in turn, see British vessels in the Red Sea as a legitimate target, the repercussions will likely compound the UK’s economic woes. 

It seems like the government is walking a very thin line that the Houthis will be keeping a keen eye on.

RELATED

Starmer ‘complicit’ in Trump’s Yemen massacre

 READ MORE 

Blowback

Burnham and Pollard linked the refuelling support for Saudi Arabia to Britain’s cost of living crisis, rising fuel prices and the security of international shipping. But British military support for Saudi Arabia may well have the reverse effect.

The rationale behind the government’s decision appears detached from the context of both the current conflict in Yemen and the appalling record of civilian harm in previous US and Saudi airstrikes that Britain has supported and facilitated.

A statement from the Ministry of Defence put the onus of the reignition of Yemen’s civil war in recent weeks on “renewed Houthi attacks” with no mention of the Saudi strikes on Sana’a airport on 13 July that upended a four-year-long truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.

Much of the British media has uncritically adopted the MoD’s framing of the conflict without including key context about which side actually broke the ceasefire.

Saudi’s July strikes aimed to prevent the landing of an Iranian passenger jet carrying a Houthi delegation returning from the funeral of Iran’s Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei who was assassinated by a US-Israeli strike in March. The Saudis later allowed the plane to land safely in Hodeidah, which is also under Houthi control.

No commercial flights have operated out of Sana’a since Israeli strikes destroyed five of Yemen’s state carrier Yemenia passenger jets in May 2025. The Saudi strikes in July triggered escalating tit-for-tat attacks between the two sides and prompted the Houthis to declare a “blockade-for-blockade” on Saudi Arabia resulting in the targeting of Saudi vessels in the Red Sea.

Chokepoint

The ground war in Yemen also flared with fighting on multiple fronts between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed internationally recognised government (IRG) of Yemen. The IRG has remained largely resident in the Saudi capital Riyadh for more than a decade. 

Although there have been no parliamentary elections since 2003, the self-exiled government has strengthened its position under Saudi direction since January, following a violent fallout between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates whose allied forces had divided the anti-Houthi side.

On 10 and 11 September, the Houthis swept into IRG territory with a lightning takeover of Yemen’s south-west coast including islands in and around the Bab al-Mandab strait. 

One of the world’s most important maritime chokepoints, Bab al-Mandab has become increasingly vital since the Strait of Hormuz – on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula – was closed by the US war on Iran.

Fighting in the highlands overlooking the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab remains unrelenting with fierce battles raging over strategic mountains. Latest figures from the International Organization for Migration (IOM) put the number of people displaced from the recent violence at almost 130,000 in just a few weeks.

Following their territorial gains two weeks ago, Houthi officials were quick to assuage fears over maritime trade through the Bab al-Mandab and southern Red Sea. 

“There is no closure of the Bab al-Mandab Strait,” Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdusalam stated, adding that the naval blockade was limited to only targeting “the Saudi side.”

Houthi attacks hit over 125 ships and sank four vessels killing nine merchant mariners from 2023 to the end of 2024 during the Houthi targeting of Israeli-linked vessels in response to the war in Gaza. International shipping transiting between Asia and Europe was forced to re-route south around South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope.

Saudi Arabia had been using the southern Red Sea to bypass the closed Strait of Hormuz and export oil to Asia through its east-west pipeline from the Yanbu oil terminal on the west coast. Houthi attacks on Saudi vessels and on Yanbu ended the export of around 4 million barrels of oil per day via the alternative route.

Brent crude oil prices surged last week to over $108 per barrel on the loss of 4% of global oil exports from Yanbu. A price that has since dropped back down below the $100-a-barrel marker. But petrol and diesel prices in the UK are currently at their highest rate since the US-Israeli war on Iran began at the end of February.

While Burnham is understandably worried about rising energy prices as Britain heads into winter, there is no evidence that further bombing of the Houthis will help, given that the group has already withstood years of aerial bombardment. 

Potential Houthi repercussions for British support of Saudi bombing may make things worse by increasing the threat to UK-linked vessels in the Bab al-Mandab through which around 25% of global container trade usually passes. 

RELATED

Rishi Sunak is Ninth UK Prime Minister to Bomb Yemen...

 READ MORE 

Impunity 

Three successive Conservative prime ministers supported Saudi Arabia’s first air war against the Houthis from 2015 to 2022. 

The war resulted in more than 19,000 civilian casualties in up to 75,217 individual strikes over the seven years of bombing, according to airstrikes monitor Yemen Data Project (YDP). Saudi Arabia successfully lobbied to remove UN experts from investigating the conflict.

In October 2021, in an unprecedented move by member states, the UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC) voted down a resolution for a two-year renewal of the Group of Eminent Experts (GEE) on Yemen. 

The GEE was created in 2017 to investigate and monitor violations of human rights, international humanitarian law (IHL) and war crimes by all belligerents. It was the first time in UNHRC history for a resolution to be voted down. Saudi Arabia reportedly influenced the vote by lobbying member states using “incentives and threats”.

The GEE mandate ended on 31 October 2021, halting the only international mechanism for accountability for IHL violations in the conflict.

In the three months following the UNHRC vote, civilian casualties in Saudi’s air war more than trebled every month, taking the monthly average of civilian casualties in bombings after October 2021 to 141, compared to less than six per month in the 12 months preceding the dissolution of the GEE, according to YDP records.

Adding to Saudi Arabia’s documented track record of civilian harm and accountability prevention is an absence of any record keeping or process for assessing civilian casualties by the British Ministry of Defence. 

Yet Pollard asserted in one of his BBC interviews on Tuesday that all British actions would “be compliant with international humanitarian law”.

One of the beneficiaries of Saudi’s renewed conflict in Yemen is likely to be British arms manufacturer BAE Systems who made at least £2.3 billion every year from contracts with the Saudi military during the 2015–2022 air campaign.

That is according to BAE data highlighted by the Campaign Against the Arms Trade in a recent report proposing reparations for Yemen funded by a windfall tax on British arms companies that enabled Saudi’s devastating bombing campaign.

The post What the media isn’t telling you about Burnham’s support for Saudi Arabia appeared first on Declassified UK.

item.title: Labour council’s Palantir shares soar as by-election looms
item.dc:creator: PAUL HOLDEN
item.description:
Exclusive: Disclosure comes as Labour’s candidate in Camden faces off with Greens

The post Labour council’s Palantir shares soar as by-election looms appeared first on Declassified UK.
item.content:encoded:
Camden Council’s investments in Palantir, the controversial AI company with ties to the Israeli military, have increased by over 1,200% since October 2023.

The council’s overall holdings in companies complicit in Israel’s violation of Palestinian rights have risen in value by almost 30 percent – worth £28 million – since June 2024

The surge in value is exposed in new Freedom of Information disclosures provided to the Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC) and shared exclusively with Declassified.

The more than 60 companies in question have been identified by PSC as those which are providing products, equipment and services used by Israel in breaches of international law and human rights.

The dramatic rise comes as Camden Council leader Sagal Abdi-Wali is standing as the Labour Party’s candidate in the heated Holborn and St Pancras by-election.

It is Keir Starmer’s former constituency and includes significant portions of Camden, where  the council has largely ignored widespread public protests and demands for divestment since 2024.

The value of the council’s holdings in Palantir grew from £276,444 to £3.65m in the period between October 2023 and December 2025.

Additional FOI disclosures from late 2024 show that the biggest increase in Camden’s investments in Palantir occurred between September 2024 and December 2025. The value of Camden’s shareholding increased from £683,045.88 to £3.65m in this period.

Palantir entered into a highly controversial strategic partnership with the Israeli Ministry of Defence in January 2024.

There have also been widespread calls for the UK government to cancel numerous contracts Palantir holds with the NHS and other government departments.

This May, London’s Mayor Sadiq Khan blocked the Metropolitan Police awarding a £50m contract to the company founded by billionaire Peter Thiel who has said that freedom and democracy are “no longer compatible”.

Camden’s holdings also include over £10m invested in defence companies providing weapons and supplies to the Israel Defense Forces. This includes shares in Boeing (£1.69m), Lockheed Martin (£1.12m) and Israeli drone manufacturer Elbit Systems (£46,837).

Camden, the large central London borough, has over £2.4bn under investment through its Local Government Pension Fund (LGPF). The fund invests money for Camden Council employees, usually by subscribing to funds run by asset managers such as Baillie Gifford and Legal & General. 

The PSC has campaigned since 2025 to force the government to ensure that similar local government schemes use screening tools to prevent investments in companies complicit with Israel’s occupation and genocide.

As part of the campaign, PSC has used Freedom of Information requests to establish the content and value of shareholdings held by LGPFs. PSC used the first disclosure from Camden, dated June 2024, to determine that Camden held £104m in companies complicit with Israeli occupation and genocide.

The latest disclosure which covers the value of the shareholdings up to the end of 2025, shows that they have increased to £133.5 million.

An analysis of the disclosures indicates that the increase in value is due to both the increased value of the shares held by Camden and the purchase of additional shareholdings in complicit companies.

Lewis Backon, PSC campaigns officer, said: “It is beyond shameful that, in the face of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and atrocities across Palestine, Camden council is continuing to funnel many millions of pounds of workers’ deferred wages into companies making these crimes possible.”

RELATED

Palantir UK chief walks away from Gaza genocide questions

 READ MORE 

Ignoring calls for divestment

The growth in the value of Camden’s shareholding has happened despite widespread public calls for divestment.

The calls began in late 2024, when Lorna Russell – who was then the sole Green Party councillor on Camden council – attempted to move a motion calling for the pension fund to divest from complicit companies.

Russell was unable to find any other councillors to second the motion, which meant it was not heard in the council chamber. The council is controlled by the Labour Party, which has long had an outright majority of councillors in the borough.

Camden’s rules, however, allowed that the motion would have to be debated if a petition containing 4,000 signatures was presented.

In January 2025, campaigners from Camden Friends of Palestine delivered a petition with over 4,000 signatures, urging the council to conduct an audit of the fund with a view to divestment.

The debate took place in January 2025 as hundreds of protestors lined the street outside the council chambers while campaigners held signs and called from the public gallery.

Lorna Russell was the only councillor to argue for divestment, although the Labour Councillor Awale Olad called out the humanitarian crisis in Gaza in a later session.

Months later, Olad, a councillor of fifteen years, decided not to stand for re-election as a Labour councillor.

He told the Labour Party of his decision in a stinging letter released to the local press. “I alone stood up and spoke out against the horrifying situation [in Gaza]”, Olad explained.

Russell told Declassified that the figures reported here “raise serious questions” about whether the responsible investment policy Camden claims to have is actually working.

“In a two-year period when divestment has been a key political issue, it is astounding that the value of Camden’s investment in Palantir has increased more than tenfold,” she said.

“Camden’s approach to engagement is evidently not working and our money is increasingly being invested in companies whose activities conflict with our values.”

She added: “Divestment is the only way to ensure that our pension fund does not profit from practices we would condemn publicly, and must be implemented as soon as possible.”

Labour candidate’s silence

Camden council leader and by-election candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali is running against Green Party leader Zack Polanski.

Abdi-Wali, who was raised in Camden by Somali refugee parents, has said that Starmer was “really inspirational”.

In a recent interview in the New Statesman, Abdi-Wali said that “people really value” the work Starmer had done as an MP and that he had “given his life to social justice.”

Abdi-Wali was first elected as a councillor in 2022 in the safe Labour ward of Camden Square.

She was selected by the Labour Party to stand in the ward after the previous councillor, Ranjit Singh, was effectively blocked and dissuaded from standing.

He was one of seven councillors blocked by the Starmerite local machinery in moves that were widely described as a ‘purge’ of left-wing and independent-minded councillors.

Abdi-Wali’s record on Gaza and divestment became a flashpoint in the council chamber a week ago.

Protestors in the gallery responded with upset when the council failed to debate a new motion on divestment.

A protestor from Camden Friends of Palestine read a statement from the gallery accusing Abdi-Wali of “refusing to speak about divestment even once during your time as councillor.” A video of the incident went viral on social media.

A review of Abdi-Wali’s social media and other public sources indicate that she does not appear to have written about or mentioned Gaza at any stage between 7 October 2023 and her selection as Labour’s MP candidate.

Abdi-Wali did not respond to Declassified’s requests to provide copies of statements or comments she has made on Gaza since her election as a councillor.

Abdi-Wali notably failed to sign up to PSC’s Candidate Pledge campaign, which was launched ahead of council elections held across the country in May 2026. The pledge committed council candidates to ensuring their local councils were not complicit in genocide and to undertake divestment.

Over 200 Labour council candidates signed the pledge, including 30 Labour candidates in the borough of Islington.

In neighbouring Camden, 43 candidates signed on, including a raft of Green and independent candidates. However, no Labour candidate from Camden joined them.

Abdi-Wali was made the leader of Camden Council in May 2026. She was proposed for the position by the Chief Whip of the Labour Group, Izzy Lenga.

Lenga, like Abdi-Wali, was selected for a safe Labour seat in 2022. In March 2021, Electronic Intifada revealed that Lenga had been photographed wearing an Israeli army uniform, draped in the Israeli flag and holding a rifle.

Camden council has long featured high-profile members of the pro-Israel Jewish Labour Movement (JLM). JLM, which was fiercely critical of Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership of the Labour Party, is affiliated with the British subsidiary of the World Zionist Organisation (WZO).

In 2024, a BBC investigation established that the WZO’s ‘Settlement Division’ had provided money and support for the creation of Israeli settler outposts in the occupied West Bank.

In addition to Lenga, who is JLM’s vice president, prominent members of the group recently on the council have included the leader of the council between 2018 and 2024, Georgia Gould, and JLM’s National Secretary Rebecca Filer. Filer is one of six Labour councillors that sits on Camden’s pension committee. Gould is now a government minister.

RELATED

Oxford academic challenges secrecy around university’s endowment fund

 READ MORE 

Into the long grass

Following the public debate in January 2025, the Labour-dominated Camden Council ultimately decided to refer the matter to a specialist pension committee, which many critics believed was an attempt to kick it into the long grass.

The pension committee was dominated by Labour Party councillors, who made up six of its eight members. The other two members were drawn from the Liberal Democrats and the Tories.

In March 2025, two months after the fractious chamber debate on divestment, the Labour-dominated council amended its constitution to limit the scope of protests in the chamber, including passing a new rule to prevent people holding signs or banners in the public gallery.

The chamber had previously been temporarily closed after silent protestors had held up signs reading ‘end the genocide.’ The moves were attacked by the Greens and Lib Dems.

Minutes of the council’s specialist pension committee show that it finally produced the details of an audit of the LGPF in December 2025, nearly a year after it had been referred to the committee.

The council hired an outside firm to conduct the audit which determined that only £15.9m of Camden’s shareholdings, held across 46 companies, were exposed to significant human rights violation concerns related to conflict zones.

Responding to Declassified’s findings, a Camden Council spokesperson said: “We have always been open and transparent about how the pension fund is invested and we’re fully committed to our responsible investment principles.

“While there has not been a separate vote on the specific divestment proposal, the Pension Committee has carefully considered the issues raised and has taken a number of steps to strengthen the fund’s approach to responsible investment. We have a duty to act with the best long-term financial interests of members but, alongside this, we also expect environmental issues, social values, and human rights to play a central role in decision-making.

“Like all Local Government Pension Scheme funds, we operate within wider investment pooling arrangements, which means changes to portfolios can take time to implement. However, the Fund has made significant progress in recent years by strengthening its responsible investment approach, increasing sustainable investment, and reviewing exposure to investments that present environmental, social and governance risks.”

The post Labour council’s Palantir shares soar as by-election looms appeared first on Declassified UK.

item.title: Oxford academic challenges secrecy around university’s endowment fund
item.dc:creator: DANIA AKKAD
item.description:
Are fund managers investing Oxford’s money in companies linked to Israeli military operations? A tribunal will decide who has the right to know

The post Oxford academic challenges secrecy around university’s endowment fund appeared first on Declassified UK.
item.content:encoded:
Is the public entitled to know exactly where Oxford University invests billions of pounds of its endowment – and if that includes firms profiting from Israeli military operations?

This is the question now facing a tribunal, following a legal challenge brought by an Oxford climate scientist and heard over two days in a cramped, airless courtroom in London last week.

In May 2024, Dr Ellen Dyer filed a Freedom of Information request with Oxford University Endowment Management (OUEM), which oversees the Oxford Endowment Fund.

The vast majority of Oxford’s £4.2bn central endowment is invested in this fund, along with most of the university’s colleges and several British charities. 

What Oxford does is significant. The total value of the collegiate university – the central endowment plus the funds of individual colleges – is understood to be the largest of any British university.

Nine months into Israel’s war on Gaza, as university campuses became flash points for pro-Palestinian activism and boycott campaigns, Dyer wanted to know: what was the value of OEF’s holdings in Elbit Systems, Rolls-Royce Holdings and Caterpillar. 

All three companies are on the Boycott Divestment and Sanctions campaign’s divestment shortlist. 

Elbit is Israel’s largest arms firm, Rolls-Royce manufacturers and supplies engines and power-pack systems used by the Israeli military and Caterpillar’s heavy machinery is used by the Israeli military to demolish Palestinian homes.

A month after her request, the OUEM responded, refusing to confirm or deny whether it held the information, a decision later upheld by the Information Commissioners Office – and appealed by Dyer.

This January, 10 months before the appeal was heard, OUEM disclosed what Dyer had been asking for: the OEF, at the time of her request, had around £16,000 invested in Elbit Systems, £150,000 in Rolls-Royce and none in Caterpillar. 

So the tribunal hearing last week focused on the principles of the matter, rather than the release of the information she had sought.

RELATED

The UK charities sending nearly £2 million to illegal settlements

 READ MORE 

Returns vs Debate 

OUEM argues that disclosing the types of details that Dyer requested could risk exposing the strategies of the third-party fund managers who directly invest OEF’s money.

In turn, that could turn fund managers off from working with OUEM and harm its ability “to work with the best and get the best returns,” argued Robin Hopkins, OUEM’s barrister.

“If the door closed on us by a small number or even one, that would be harmful,” Hopkins said.

“If our returns start to drop, we lose, but so do the 46 charitable endowments that invest in us. Less return for us means less value for them.”

Neil Hayes, the OUEM’s general counsel, said his organisation sought the “ruby in the dust” of fund managers in a competitive market. 

That strategy has been successful, allowing it to achieve returns of five percent above inflation for investors, a target that holds “irrespective of what the market is doing”.

Dyer’s barristers contend that the risks painted by OUEM of the damage that could be done to the fund are overblown and poorly evidenced.

They pointed to only one email the OUEM shared in evidence sent from a fund manager in December 2025 who had learned about the FOI dispute and wrote to underline that he valued the confidentiality of his fund. 

“You don’t have reams of evidence to grapple with and engage with fund managers to agree or disbelieve. You don’t have past scenarios about whether they would occur,” said Tom Tabori. 

He questioned why OEUM had gone ahead and released the information sought by Dyer ahead of the tribunal, despite the apparent risks of driving the OEF’s fund managers away.

“If you were willing to disclose it in Jan 2026, presumably you should have been willing to disclose it in May 2024,” Tabori said. OUEM said that it had established by then that the information was no longer commercially sensitive.

Tabori said even if the risk of potentially losing fund managers was established, the value of the information being shared with the public to debate “whether a £6bn fund owned by a public authority should go in this direction” should outweigh it.

“It’s not about the merits, if you like, of the investment. It’s to enable those merits to be debated,” Tabori said.

Digging for information

Dyer’s FOI was among over 150 such requests filed by the Oxford BDS Coalition since October 2023. 

Their goal was to try to find out if and how much of Oxford’s endowment is invested in arms companies or firms operating or complicit in the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territories.

During this period, the coalition learned that the university has indirect investments, worth more than £19 million, in at least 49 companies flagged by the UN and human rights organisations for their involvement in illegal Israeli activities in the occupied territories.

The investments are made through a passive equity tracker fund that was purposefully developed by BlackRock and the university in 2020 to screen out firms involved in fossil fuels and controversial weapons.

But the vast majority of the university’s company-level holdings have remained a mystery because the OEF, which holds most of the endowment, doesn’t disclose that level of detail to the public.

OUEM made clear in the tribunal that investors in the fund can get that kind of detail if they ask for it, but that it cannot be shared with the public. 

“You get it on confidential terms,” Hopkins said. “You get it in a way that means you may not be able to share with all of your college fellows or staff members.”

Clearly, that would not satisfy Dyer or the coalition who have waited years for the information to be released so that it can be publicly scrutinised. 

Tribunal Judge Gilda Kiai concluded the two-day hearing asking both parties for patience. “This is going to be a very difficult decision to make. It may take me a while,” she said.

The post Oxford academic challenges secrecy around university’s endowment fund appeared first on Declassified UK.

item.title: Israel killed three UK citizens. Now their families want answers
item.dc:creator: JOHN McEVOY
item.description:
A coroner’s court has been asked to investigate Israel’s aid worker massacre and review surveillance tapes held by Britain’s military

The post Israel killed three UK citizens. Now their families want answers appeared first on Declassified UK.
item.content:encoded:
A pre-inquest review opened today into the killing of three British citizens working as security consultants for World Central Kitchen (WCK) in Gaza.

James ‘Jim’ Henderson, 33, James Kirby, 47, and John Chapman, 57, were among seven aid workers killed in a series of Israeli drone strikes on 1 April 2024.

Then UK prime minister Rishi Sunak told Benjamin Netanyahu he was “appalled” by the incident while current foreign secretary Ed Miliband described the killings as “cold-blooded”.

Nochi Mendel, the colonel who ordered the strike, said he is “not sorry” and the Israeli military recently announced it would not pursue any criminal investigations.

At Avon Coroner’s Court in Bristol, lawyers for the aid workers’ families demanded a full investigation into the incident including the actions and policies of the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) as well as the munitions used.

They want the inquest to establish whether the aid workers were unlawfully killed and whether the strikes were conducted in accordance with Israel’s targeting and deconfliction policies, with the coroner already indicating she will include the IDF and Mendel as interested persons.

The families have also requested that enquiries be made to Britain’s Ministry of Defence (MoD) amid questions about intelligence sharing with Israel, with a view to also including that department as an interested person.

This comes after Declassified revealed a British surveillance aircraft overflew Gaza shortly before the attack, with the UK government refusing to release the footage or even disclose the aircraft’s flight path.

In a statement outside the court, the Kirby family said: “The coroner told us today that Colonel Mendel, the Israeli military and the Israeli government are going to be made interested persons in this inquest.

“We also have questions for the British government. An RAF surveillance plane was flying over Gaza on the day James died. The Ministry of Defence has the footage from that flight but will not tell us whether it shows the area where the convoy was hit. We think the coroner should be given it.

“We are now asking the Government to give the Coroner whatever it has, and to keep pressing Israel for the drone footage and the other evidence. If Israel says no, people should be told that.

“There is no other independent investigation into James’ death. This inquest is all we have, and we are going to see it through”.

The massacre

Over the past two years, an Australian government investigation alongside various media and firsthand accounts have shed light on what happened the night of the attack.

Shortly after 11pm local time, the aid workers were targeted by three Israeli drone strikes launched roughly four minutes apart while travelling in a WCK convoy towards Rafah.

Earlier that evening, the convoy had escorted aid trucks from a makeshift pier to the WCK welcome centre in Deir el-Balah, where locally contracted security guards boarded the vehicles, according to the Australian investigation. 

Some of those local guards were armed, according to IDF officers who were monitoring the operation from above with surveillance drones, with one allegedly firing a gun into the air.

The IDF claimed the presence of the local guards indicated a hijacking by Hamas, despite the convoy continuing along its planned route and unloading the aid at a WCK warehouse some three miles south.

After unloading the aid, IDF drones continued to watch from the skies as the WCK convoy departed west towards the coastal road while a car carrying the local guards drove north.

The WCK convoy was supposed to return via the welcome centre, but a decision was made to travel directly to the accommodation in Rafah due to the operation being delayed, according to the Australian investigation.

While this amounted to a modification in the route, it did not impact the decision to target the convoy because the IDF only became aware of this diversion later on.

The IDF says it then “mistakenly believed that the vehicles” travelling south “contained Hamas military operatives and therefore struck the vehicles”, with one account suggesting a bag put into one of the WCK vehicles was erroneously thought to be a weapon.

When the airstrikes were launched, the WCK convoy was nowhere near any Israeli troops and posed no reasonable threat to the IDF. 

In written submissions to the coroner’s court, lawyers for the Henderson family argued the IDF’s narrative is “contradicted by all of the available evidence”.

“At its highest”, they wrote, “there was an alleged mistaken identification of a bag being placed into one of the cars being a gun or containing a gun”.

Pete Weatherby, representing the Henderson family, noted how the lawyers were “piecing together from open source material either from Mendel or the Israeli official position different and not entirely consistent narratives”.

He said it would therefore be useful for the Israeli government to finally outline “what they say actually happened factually as a starting point for the investigation”.

The strikes were “intentionally lethal”, lawyers added in written submissions, “and the postmortem finding shows that Jim’s injuries were so severe they resulted in his immediate death”.

When asked about WCK, Mendel previously said: “Unfortunately, they aren’t really a neutral organisation. Not really an organisation you can say is innocent and completely clean… It has ties to Hamas”.

Scope of the inquest

Given Israel’s failure to provide a full account of the incident or pursue a criminal investigation, lawyers for the families have requested that the coroner launch a thorough and independent investigation into how the deaths came about.

The investigation, they contend, should go beyond the immediate circumstances of the incident to the IDF’s policies on targeting and deconfliction with the goal of determining whether the aid workers were killed unlawfully.

This is particularly important within the context of the IDF carrying out a pattern of strikes on aid convoys and premises during the six months prior to the WCK massacre.

“It appears prima facie that this is a case where three British citizens (and others) were unlawfully killed by the military of an allied nation”, the Hendersons’ lawyers argued in written submissions.

They pointed to a recent investigation in the Guardian which found the WCK strikes were “in line with a general policy employed by the Israeli military of… ‘incrimination’, which gives commanders in the field wide discretion on designating someone as a ‘terrorist’.”

The coroner’s court also heard that the strikes were launched with a Hermes 450 drone, alleged by Campaign Against Arms Trade (CAAT) to be powered by UK-made engines.

“There has been a great deal of public concern around the possibility that UK manufactured components or UK based research and development contributed to the killing of Jim and his colleagues”, the lawyers submitted.

Establishing the source of weaponry used in the attack is therefore “central” to understanding how the aid workers came to their death and “should be investigated”.

The lawyers also pointed to how an inquest jury previously found Tom Hurndall, another British national who died in Gaza in 2006, had been “unlawfully and intentionally killed” by the IDF.

Surveillance footage 

The lawyers also requested that Britain’s MoD disclose whether it holds relevant surveillance or intelligence data relating to the incident.

The MoD previously informed Declassified that it holds video surveillance footage of Gaza from the day of the aid worker massacre but is refusing to publish the tape.

The footage was taken by a RAF surveillance plane which spent approximately five hours above the strip that day, returning to base shortly before the airstrikes took place.

The MoD may therefore have collected footage of events leading up to the tragedy, which could provide clarity over Israeli claims regarding Hamas “gunmen” near the convoy.

To this end, lawyers submitted that “the British Ministry of Defence… should be given the opportunity to be interested persons in these inquest proceedings”.

The lawyers specifically noted how any footage taken over Gaza that day “is obviously potentially relevant, and may show the progress and actions of the convoy”.

The coroner suggested that initial questions will be put to the MoD before deciding whether to include the department as an interested person.

Further information was requested from the Foreign Office with regard to what measures were in place to keep British aid workers in Gaza safe prior to April 2024, and what additional actions have been taken since the incident.

Elbit Systems has also been recommended as an interested person given the company could provide a witness statement confirming “whether any part of the [drone] originated in the UK”.

“As you know Elbit operates 16 facilities in the UK, the centrepiece is very close to where we are now in Bristol,” the lawyers said today.

“In terms of allaying public concern we would say this is a key part of this particular inquisitorial process and therefore evidence should be obtained from Elbit and they should be invited to take part in the process”.

In addition, the coroner has been requested to seek disclosure of IDF drone footage and audio, the IDF’s investigation file, IDF policy and procedures documents, and internal material from WCK.

The Foreign Office recently announced: “The World Central Kitchen attack is one of countless incidents in Gaza where there has been no accountability. In Gaza, humanitarian workers continue to work tirelessly to support civilians in desperate need, risking their lives whilst working in the most perilous conditions. 

“Yet despite the fragile ceasefire, Gaza remains the deadliest place to deliver aid, with 186 humanitarian workers killed in 2025. Israel must comply with its obligations under international humanitarian law, and must do more to ensure that humanitarian staff can carry out their work safely. Lessons must be learnt from this tragedy”.

The coroner is now expected to seek disclosure from interested persons as well as other relevant parties before a second pre-inquest review takes place on 5 March 2027.
